All at once Mr. Podgers released Lord Arthur’s right hand and took his left, stooping so closely over it that the golden rims of his spectacles appeared almost to brush the palm. For an instant his face was a pallid mask of terror; then he regained his composure and, raising his eyes to Lady Windermere, observed with a constrained smile, ‘It is the hand of a most charming young man.

‘Naturally it is!’ Lady Windermere replied. ‘But is he to make a charming husband? That is what I wish to hear.’

‘All charming young men do,’ answered Mr. Podgers.

‘I should not wish a husband to be too fascinating,’ Lady Jedburgh murmured thoughtfully. ‘It is so very dangerous.’

‘My dear child, they are never too fascinating,’ exclaimed Lady Windermere. ‘But I am asking for particulars. Particulars are the only interesting things. What is to happen to Lord Arthur?’

‘Well, before many months have passed, Lord Arthur will undertake a voyage—’

‘Oh, yes—his honeymoon, naturally!’

‘And suffer the loss of a relative.’

‘Not his sister, I trust?’ asked Lady Jedburgh in a plaintive voice.

‘Certainly not his sister,’ Mr. Podgers replied, waving a hand in gentle protest. ‘Only a distant relation.’

‘Well, I am terribly disappointed,’ said Lady Windermere. ‘I have nothing whatever to tell Sybil tomorrow. Nobody troubles about distant relations nowadays. They ceased to be fashionable years ago. Still, I suppose she ought to have some black silk ready; one can always wear it to church, you know. And now we must go down to supper. They will surely have eaten everything, but perhaps there is some hot soup left. François once made admirable soup, but politics have excited him so much lately that I never feel quite sure of him. I do wish General Boulanger would remain quiet. Duchess, you must be tired?’

‘Not in the least, dear Gladys,’ replied the Duchess, waddling towards the door. ‘I have enjoyed myself exceedingly, and the chiropodist—I mean the chiromantist—is most interesting. Flora, what has become of my tortoiseshell fan? Oh, Sir Thomas, thank you so much. And my lace shawl, Flora? Oh, thank you, Sir Thomas; you are very kind indeed.’ The good creature eventually contrived to reach the floor below without dropping her scent-bottle more than twice.

Throughout this conversation Lord Arthur Savile had stood beside the fireplace, oppressed by the same dread, the same sickening anticipation of evil. As his sister swept past on Lord Plymdale’s arm, beautiful in pink brocade and pearls, he gave her a melancholy smile. He scarcely heard Lady Windermere calling him to follow. His thoughts were with Sybil Merton, and the possibility that anything might part them brought a mist of tears to his eyes.

“Keeping firmly before us the particulars to which I have directed your notice—the singular voice, the extraordinary agility, and the astonishing want of motive for a murder of such exceptional atrocity—let us consider the slaughter itself. A woman has been strangled by the strength of hands and forced head foremost up a chimney. Common murderers do not kill in this fashion; still less do they dispose of their victims so. You must admit that this thrusting of the corpse into the chimney has something excessively strange about it, something wholly at variance with our ordinary conception of human conduct, even if we imagine the persons concerned to be the most abandoned of men. Reflect also upon the strength required to drive a body up that opening with such force that several people together could scarcely pull it down.

“Consider next the other signs of a most extraordinary exertion of strength. Upon the hearth lay thick locks—exceedingly thick locks—of grey human hair, torn out by the roots. You know the considerable force required to wrench even twenty or thirty hairs at once from the head. You examined those locks as I did. Fragments of the scalp still clung to their roots—a dreadful sight, and certain evidence of the enormous power employed in tearing out perhaps half a million hairs together. The elderly woman’s throat had not simply been cut: her head had been completely separated from her body, and the weapon was nothing more than a razor. Notice, too, the brutal savagery of these acts. I pass over the bruises on Madame L’Espanaye’s body. Monsieur Dumas and his estimable colleague Monsieur Etienne have declared them to be the work of a blunt instrument, and in this they are entirely right. That instrument was plainly the stone paving of the courtyard, upon which the victim fell from the window overlooking the bed. Simple as this explanation may now appear, the police missed it for the very reason that they overlooked the width of the shutters: the matter of the nails had completely closed their minds to the possibility that the windows could ever have been opened.

“If, together with all this, you have duly considered the chamber’s peculiar disorder, we have now brought into conjunction these ideas: astonishing agility, strength beyond the human, savage ferocity, slaughter without motive, a grotesqueness of horror wholly foreign to humanity, and a voice whose tone was unfamiliar to listeners of many nations, and which contained no distinct or intelligible articulation of syllables.”

Smallpox!

I rushed to the king and whispered in his ear:

“Get out of here immediately, Your Majesty! The woman is dying of the disease that devastated the outskirts of Camelot two years ago.”

He did not move.

“I will certainly stay—and help as well.”

I whispered again:

“King, you cannot do this. You must leave.”

“You mean well, and your advice is sensible. But it would disgrace a king to show fear, and disgrace a knight to refuse help where people need it. Enough. I will not leave. You are the one who must go. The Church’s ban does not apply to me, but it forbids you to be here. If word of your offence reaches the Church, it will punish you severely.”

He was in terrible danger, and staying might cost him his life, but arguing would accomplish nothing. If he believed his honour as a knight was involved, discussion was over. He would remain, and nothing could stop him. I knew that, so I let the matter drop. The woman spoke:

“Kind sir, would you please climb that ladder and tell me what you find? Do not be afraid to tell me the truth. There are times when even a mother’s heart can no longer break, because it is already broken.”

“Stay here,” the king said, “and give the woman something to eat. I will go.” He set down the knapsack.

I turned to go, but the king had already moved. He stopped and looked down at a man lying in the dim light, who had neither noticed us nor spoken.

“Is this your husband?” the king asked.

“Yes.”

“Is he asleep?”

“Thank God for that one mercy—yes, these past three hours. How can I ever express all my gratitude? My heart is bursting with thanks for the sleep he is sleeping now.”

I said:

“We will be careful. We won’t wake him.”

“No, you will not, for he is dead.”

“Dead?”

“Yes—and what a victory it is to know that! No one can hurt him now, or insult him again. He is in heaven and happy; or, if he is not there, he is in hell and content, because he will find neither abbot nor bishop in that place. We were children together. We were husband and wife for twenty-five years, never separated until today. Think how long that is to love and suffer together. This morning he was delirious. In his imagination we were a boy and girl again, wandering through happy fields. And as he talked with that innocent delight, he wandered farther and farther, still chatting happily, until he entered those other fields we know nothing of and passed beyond mortal sight.
